title: Describing people
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Spanish describes a feature with TENER, not with ser: tiene el pelo largo, and for age tiene diez años. English says "has long hair" and then switches to "is ten" — Spanish uses the same verb for both.
tener is irregular in the I-form and stem-changing everywhere else: tengo · tienes · tiene. The e→ie is the same change as quiero and quieres, and the odd one out is tengo.
The feature takes the definite article where English wants a possessive: tiene EL pelo largo, not su pelo. The hair is already known to be theirs.

With a character adjective, ser and estar do not differ in strength — they differ in MEANING. es listo is clever; está listo is ready. The L1 rule holds: ser classifies what someone is, estar reports the state they are in.
An adjective ending in -o has four shapes and one ending in -e or a consonant has two: alto · alta · altos · altas, but amable · amables and joven · jóvenes. M3 walks the whole grid.
Family words work as they do in English — mi hermano, mi padre — and mi never changes for the gender of what is owned. Only a plural moves it: mis hermanos.
mayor means older of a person, and it is also the comparative of grande. There is no más viejo in ordinary speech about a person; mayor is the word.

sentences.display: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
sentences.cue: I have a brother and a sister.
sentences.literal: I-have a brother and a sister.

words.note: tener, to have. The I-form is the odd one — tengo, with a g nobody predicts — and the rest change e→ie: tienes, tiene. The dictionary form is tener.
The partner of M4's hermana. hermanos covers brothers, and also brothers and sisters together — a mixed group takes the masculine plural.

sentences.trap: hermanos is not only "brothers". Ask ¿Tienes hermanos? and you are asking about siblings of either kind.
sentences.sound: TEN-go, hard g as in "go". er-MA-no, with the h completely silent.

variations.changed: a number, and only sisters
the shortest the sentence gets

variations.cue: I don't have any brothers or sisters.
variations.changed: no in front, and the article disappears with it

mistake.why: The I-form of tener is tengo. The g is not optional and there is no rule to derive it from — it is learnt.

sentences.usage: The first question anyone asks a newcomer, and the first answer they give.
sentences.mnemonic: tengo hides a g; every other form hides an ie.

words.note: Four shapes, and the one you write tracks the person: mi hermano es alto, mi hermana es alta. It also means high of a thing, and loud of a voice.

sentences.trap: The adjective follows the noun everywhere else, but after es it simply sits at the end: es alto. There is nothing for it to follow.
sentences.sound: AL-to. The l is clear and forward, never the dark English l of "tall".

variations.changed: the adjective follows the person, not the speaker
everything goes plural together — mis, son, altos

variations.display: Mi hermano no es muy alto.
variations.changed: no in front of the verb, and muy stays put

mistake.why: The adjective agrees with the person it describes: alta. Who is speaking makes no difference at all.

sentences.usage: Neutral description. Spanish is comfortable saying it about someone present, in a way English often is not.
sentences.mnemonic: The ending points at the person, never at the speaker.

sentences.display: Mi hermana tiene el pelo largo.
sentences.literal: My sister has the hair long.

words.note: The he-she-usted form of tener, and the verb Spanish uses for features: tiene el pelo largo. The row for tener is S01's.
Singular, always, for the hair on a head: el pelo. A pelos plural would be individual hairs off it.
Length only. It is not English "large" — that is grande — and mistaking the two is the commonest false friend in the language.

sentences.trap: el pelo, not su pelo. Spanish leaves the possessive out when the owner is already the subject of the sentence.
sentences.sound: PE-lo, with a single tapped r nowhere in it — do not import the rr of perro.

variations.display: Mi hermano tiene el pelo corto.
variations.changed: the opposite length, same frame
the same sentence about yourself
the tú form, asked as a question

mistake.why: A feature takes tener, not ser: tiene el pelo largo. ser would be claiming she IS hair.

sentences.usage: Everyday description. Hair, eyes and height are all tener; character is ser.
sentences.mnemonic: In Spanish you HAVE the hair; in English you ARE the hairstyle.

sentences.display: Mi madre tiene el pelo corto.
sentences.literal: My mother has the hair short.

words.note: Feminine and ending in -e: la madre, las madres. Mamá is what most people actually call her.
Short in LENGTH. A short person is bajo, not corto, and the two are never interchangeable.

sentences.trap: corto and bajo split what English calls "short": corto is length, bajo is height.
sentences.sound: MA-dre, with the dre said as one quick beat — not ma-de-re.

variations.display: Mi padre tiene el pelo corto.
variations.changed: the other parent, same description

variations.display: Mi madre no tiene el pelo largo.
variations.cue: My mother doesn't have long hair.
variations.changed: the negative, with no in front of the verb
tener doing plain possession

mistake.why: For height the word is baja. corta would be describing her length, as of a piece of string.

sentences.usage: Neutral. Spanish family words are used far more often than English ones inside a conversation.

words.note: Masculine: el padre. padres is also the word for parents — the mixed pair takes the masculine plural, as hermanos does.
Warm and easy to be around. It is NOT English "sympathetic", which is comprensivo — one of the two or three false friends a Spanish learner meets first.

sentences.trap: simpático says nothing about compassion. It is about being good company.
sentences.sound: sim-PA-ti-co — the accent is written and it moves the stress off the syllable you would guess.

variations.changed: the ending follows the person described
padres as parents, and everything goes plural
M1's amable, which has one shape for either gender

mistake.why: An -o adjective agrees with the person: simpática. The accent stays where it is in every shape.

sentences.usage: The default compliment about a person's character, and it is used constantly.
sentences.mnemonic: simpático is good company, not a shoulder to cry on.

sentences.cue: Do you have brothers or sisters?

words.note: The tú form of tener, with the e→ie the whole verb shares except tengo. The row for tener is S01's.
One letter, and it behaves exactly as English "or" does. It becomes u before a word starting with o- to keep the two apart.

sentences.trap: No article before hermanos. Asking whether someone has any of a thing leaves the article out altogether.
sentences.sound: TYE-nes. The o of "or" is a single clean vowel and never slides into ow.

variations.cue: Do you have brothers or sisters? (polite)
variations.changed: the usted form, which looks like he or she

variations.cue: Do you have a brother or a sister?
variations.changed: the articles come back when you mean exactly one
the answer, with the article still absent

mistake.why: The definite article would be asking about particular brothers you both know. ¿Tienes hermanos? asks whether any exist.

sentences.usage: Small talk anywhere. In Spain the answer usually arrives with names and ages attached.
sentences.mnemonic: Any of a thing takes no article at all.

words.note: Masculine and feminine both exist and you pick by who the friend is: mi amigo, mi amiga.
With ser it means clever. With estar it means ready — and it is the clearest case in the language of the two verbs changing a word's meaning rather than its strength.

sentences.trap: es listo and está listo are not the same claim about the same quality. One is a mind, the other is a state of preparation.
sentences.sound: LIS-to, with the s never buzzed — closer to the ss of "lesson".

variations.changed: a female friend, and the adjective follows her
estar, and the meaning changes completely
plural throughout

mistake.why: estar makes it "ready", which is not what you meant. Cleverness is what someone IS: es listo.

sentences.usage: A compliment. In parts of Latin America listo alone is also "done, all set", said as a whole sentence.
sentences.mnemonic: ser makes a mind, estar makes a state of readiness — the same word, two jobs.

words.note: estar reporting a state, exactly as in M2's estoy bien. Here it turns listo from clever into ready. The row for estar is L1-M2's.

sentences.trap: The pair to hold together: mi amigo es listo, el café está listo. Same adjective, two verbs, two unrelated meanings.
sentences.sound: es-TA, stressed on the last syllable and written with an accent to say so.

variations.changed: a feminine thing, so the adjective moves
the negative, with no in front of está
asked as a question, with the subject moved to the end

mistake.why: ser would be calling the coffee clever. A state of readiness is always estar.

sentences.usage: Kitchens, counters, waiting rooms. The most useful está sentence there is.
sentences.mnemonic: Coffee is never clever; it is only ever ready.

words.note: Older of a person, and one shape for either gender. Spanish does not say más viejo about family; mayor is the word, and M9 will use it as the comparative of grande too.

sentences.trap: There is no "more" in front of it. mayor already carries the comparison, exactly as English "elder" does.
sentences.sound: ma-YOR, stressed at the end; the y is the y of "yes", not a vowel.

variations.changed: the same shape for a man
the plural adds -es, the only change it makes

variations.display: Mi hermana mayor es muy simpática.
variations.cue: My older sister is very nice.
variations.changed: mayor after the noun, describing which sister

mistake.why: mayor is already a comparison. Adding más doubles it, which is exactly what English "more older" does wrong.

sentences.usage: Family talk. mayor and menor are how Spanish ranks siblings, and the age itself often never comes up.
sentences.mnemonic: mayor has the comparison built in; do not pay for it twice.

sentences.display: Es mi amiga y es muy amable.
sentences.cue: She's my friend and she's very kind.
sentences.literal: Is my friend and is very kind.

words.note: The feminine of amigo, whose row is S07's. Es mi amiga needs no ella in front: the ending already says who.

sentences.trap: Two clauses and no pronoun in either. Once the person is established Spanish keeps dropping the subject, and putting ella at the front of the second half would read as a contrast.
sentences.sound: The y between the halves is said as a short ee and joins the two clauses without a pause.

variations.display: Es mi amigo y es muy simpático.
variations.cue: He's my friend and he's very nice.
variations.changed: a male friend, and both endings follow him

variations.display: Es mi hermana y es mayor.
variations.cue: She's my sister and she's older.
variations.changed: the same shape carrying S09's word

variations.display: Es mi amiga, pero no es muy alta.
variations.cue: She's my friend, but she isn't very tall.
variations.changed: pero sets the two halves against each other

mistake.display: Ella es mi amiga y ella es muy amable.
mistake.why: Neither ella is needed, and both together sound insistent. Spanish drops the subject once it is known.

sentences.usage: Introducing someone. The two-clause shape is how a Spanish speaker actually presents a person.
sentences.mnemonic: Say who once; the endings carry the rest.
